fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Species generally become rare before they become extinct, as seen in recent Tertiary formations and in animals exterminated by humans.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: We see in many cases in the more recent tertiary formations, that rarity precedes extinction; and we know that this has been the progress of events with those animals which have been exterminated, either locally or wholly, through man’s agency.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter X, “On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings”; section “On Extinction”. Scope: species approaching extinction, fossil and recent

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch10-09: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.83

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Both fossil occupancy and modern population trends are available at useful scale. Biases weaken causal interpretation but still allow a strong test of the stated empirical regularity.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate occupancy or abundance trajectories before last appearance in fossil species and before documented modern extinctions. Test whether declining rarity occurs more often than stable or increasing abundance immediately before extinction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Occurrence counts are imperfect abundance proxies.

The Signor-Lipps effect can manufacture apparent pre-extinction rarity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.94
data existence: 0.94
discriminating power: 0.63
data adequacy: 0.73
analysis feasibility: 0.88

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Pre-extinction occupancy is a clear variable, and both fossil occurrences and Quaternary paleoecological counts exist. The classic sampling bias creates exactly the decline the claim predicts, so an uncorrected result has little discriminating power. Neotoma and a few historical series can test true abundance for a recent subset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare occupancy or occurrence counts in the interval before last appearance with counts for species that survive the same interval. A drop confined to the species that are about to disappear would support the claim; extinction from high occupancy would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The Signor-Lipps effect produces a spurious decline in records before the last appearance.

Historical cases of human extermination are documented piecemeal and are not one abundance series.

Most fossil collections record presence, so rarity is occupancy rather than population size.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.75
operationalizability: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.4
data adequacy: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.75
